prize_parts.citation: for introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, transforming the analysis of exporting, foreign investment and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: B001 is the candidate where discovery, attribution and maturity line up best in my reading. Melitz (2003) and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple (2004) replaced the representative-firm view with a model in which trade reallocates activity across heterogeneous firms. That produced testable predictions on who exports, who invests abroad and where productivity gains come from. The predictions have been tested repeatedly in firm-level data from many countries for more than two decades. Some baseline predictions are rejected in detail and the model has been extended in response, which is what a productive research programme looks like. Because the central credit sits with two people, the attribution is cleaner than in the crowded macro candidates. I have tried to hold B001 to the same standard I apply elsewhere: a clear core result, repeated empirical checking, and a durable change in how the field works. It meets that standard. After reading colleagues' openings I keep B030 and B035 as my alternatives. Both pair a clear conceptual idea with credible empirical designs, the China-shock work and the sufficient-statistics and bunching work respectively. I rank B024 lower than in my opening because several colleagues showed how diffuse its attribution is.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution at the edges. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related contributions but are not among the credited names, and Redding's quantitative and spatial extensions are arguably more than a footnote. A prize to Helpman and Melitz alone could be read as under-crediting the empirical and quantitative strands that made the framework operational. A second concern is that the welfare implications of the heterogeneous-firm framework depend on functional-form assumptions, such as the productivity distribution. Welfare conclusions are therefore less robust than the qualitative selection and reallocation predictions. Trade was also recognised in 2008, and some members may weigh that against another trade prize, although I do not think field rotation is a scientific argument.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B006 first. He argues that the BLP random-coefficients demand framework and the dynamic oligopoly methods made structural industrial organisation routine and are used in merger review, antitrust, trade and environmental policy. He also notes that the three-person limit forces a choice among Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin.
responses.response: I accept the practical reach and the maturity. Of the three BLP authors, the demand-estimation credit is among the most cleanly attributed on the list. My reservation is evidentiary. Structural IO conclusions rest heavily on functional-form and instrument assumptions, and I would want to know how well the methods predict outcomes out of sample, for example in merger retrospectives. The ballot item also bundles demand estimation, dynamic games and entry models across seven credited names, so the discovery boundary is blurrier than for B001. I rank it below B001 for now, mainly on discovery boundary and robustness evidence rather than on impact. If the committee narrows it to the demand-estimation core, I would reconsider.

responses.point: Fredriksson proposes Autor, Hanson and Katz for B030. He asks whether Katz or Dorn should take the third slot and whether the task framework and the China shock are better treated as separate achievements. He also flags overlap with the Goldin 2023 and Acemoglu 2024 prizes.
responses.response: I agree the boundary question is the real issue, and it is why I keep B030 as an alternative rather than my preferred choice. My opening proposed only Autor and Hanson, which leaves out Dorn's co-authorship of the China-shock papers. Katz's foundational skill-demand work is substantial, but he shares credit for it with a laureate from 2023, so adding him blurs the discovery. I see the China-shock evidence, with its replication and robustness debates, as the stronger and more separable achievement. Adding the task framework would draw in contributors outside the credited names. If the committee goes with B030, I would sooner define it narrowly around the trade-shock evidence than merge the two strands.

responses.point: Andersson also ranks B001 first and proposes Helpman and Melitz. He leaves Redding out because his work is a later quantitative or spatial extension. He notes that trade has not been recognised since 2008, and that Helpman might be better paired with Grossman (B047) for a different citation.
responses.response: I agree on the two-person core and on Redding. I would qualify the timing argument, since time since the last prize in a field should not stand in for scientific merit. I would rest the case on the framework's empirical track record. The Helpman-Grossman pairing is a genuine alternative framing, but it is a different achievement, and B047 is not on the shortlist. We should evaluate the firm-heterogeneity discovery as the ballot defines it and not trade Helpman's body of work across candidates. I also share his uncertainty about whether the committee would prefer to credit the quantitative lineage. I think the selection-into-exporting result is the more identifiable origin.

uncertainties: Whether Redding, or Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum (who are outside the credited names), should change the committee's view of the cleanest attribution for firm-heterogeneity trade models.
How much of the welfare and gains-from-trade conclusion depends on functional-form assumptions, and whether that weakens the case relative to the more robust qualitative predictions.
Whether B006 can be bounded to a coherent demand-estimation core, and how much out-of-sample validation exists for structural IO methods. I have not verified this independently.
How to separate the China-shock evidence from the task framework in B030, and how much of the latter is already covered by the 2023 and 2024 prizes.
I rely on the supplied openings and general knowledge, and I have not independently verified citations or priority records.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for Helpman and Melitz. The profile shows no co-authorship or institutional tie to them. My listed networks (Institute for Replication, the Harvard evolutionary-dynamics group, the SSE colleagues, Camerer, Nosek and others) do not overlap with the B001 names. I see no connection to B030 or B035 either.
